name: Treaty with the Oto and Missouri, 1833
aka: Treaty of the Otoe Village on the Platte (1833)
promises: The $2,500 annuity under the 1830 Prairie du Chien treaty continued for ten years from July 15, 1840, and the $500 annuity for farm implements likewise (Articles 2 and 3).
$500 a year for five years for schools within the tribes' territory (Article 4).

A horse mill for grinding corn, two farmers for five years and $1,000 in livestock (Articles 5 and 6); Article 7 made Articles 3 to 6 (the implements annuity, the school money, the mill, the farmers and the stock) conditional on the tribes settling in agricultural districts the President chose.

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission found the 792,000 acres the Otoe and Missouria ceded by this treaty were worth 75 cents an acre on September 21, 1833, that the tribes received $39,410.15, about 4.9 cents an acre, and that this was grossly inadequate and an unconscionable consideration. It awarded $554,589.85 for this cession ($594,000.00 less the $39,410.15 paid), part of a total award of $1,179,058.40 less offsets.

landTaken: 792,000 acres south of the Little Nemaha River, as the Commission fixed the acreage (Docket 11, finding 14 and opinion on the Third Cause of Action).
compensation: The Commission found the tribes received $39,410.15 for this cession and awarded $554,589.85 for it, within a combined award of $1,179,058.40 for this and the 1854 cession, less offsets to be determined; it allowed no interest because it found no taking in the constitutional sense (Opinion, March 31, 1953).
today: The claimant was the Otoe and Missouria Tribe of Indians, today the Otoe-Missouria Tribe of Indians in Oklahoma.

plain.promised: Continued annuities of $2,500 and $500 for ten years, school money, a corn mill, two farmers and livestock, some only if the tribes settled where the President chose, and $400 in goods at signing.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found in 1953 that the tribes received $39,410.15, about 4.9 cents an acre, for 792,000 acres worth 75 cents an acre, an unconscionable consideration.
plain.today: The Commission awarded $554,589.85 for this cession, within a $1,179,058.40 total less offsets, with no interest. Whether it was paid has not been traced.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe's own history says settlers wanted and moved onto its traditional farming lands in Nebraska, Iowa, Missouri and Kansas, that the Otoe-Missouria fought to protect them, and that the United States acted to protect the settlers until the Tribe was confined to the Big Blue River reservation in 1855.

openQuestions: The final net award after offsets was not established: the December 11, 1953 opinion on offsets (OSU id 312) is badly damaged OCR and was not read to its end figure.
The Court of Claims reviewed this docket (Otoe and Missouria Tribe v. United States, 131 Ct. Cl. 593, 1955, as commonly cited); that decision and the final net award after offsets were not opened.
The Otoe-Missouria Tribe's own account of this treaty was not looked for in this pass.

Audit 2026-11-07: the per-cession award of $554,589.85 is stated in the Commission's opinion (2 Ind. Cl. Comm. 355, OSU id 0), not only derived; the earlier note that it was the researcher's arithmetic was removed and the figure moved into the breach and compensation. Promise 3 reworded: Article 7 conditions Articles 3 to 6, not only the mill, farmers and stock.
